title: PHP2Shell: GitLab helps find and remediate critical PHP flaws
summary:
GitLab is not affected by PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619). The GitLab application is not written in PHP and does not run it to serve web requests, and our Security team has found no evidence of impact to GitLab-managed infrastructure. GitLab.com, GitLab Self-Managed, and GitLab Dedicated are not impacted.

PHP is a widely used programming language that runs on web servers and powers popular platforms like WordPress, Drupal, and Magento, so a flaw in PHP itself can affect many websites and applications. On October 21, 2026, the PHP project fixed two critical remote code execution flaws in PHP, together known as PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619). PHP rates both 9.2 on CVSS v4.0. The flaws are in the PHP engine, not in any framework, library, or application code, so there is no application-level fix. Any web server that runs PHP is affected, including NGINX and Apache. The PHP project confirmed the vulnerability on Apache with mod_php, where an unauthenticated request can achieve remote code execution before any application code runs.

Upgrade every server and container that runs PHP to serve web requests to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35, or to your distribution’s patched package now.

This guide is for security and platform teams with PHP projects on GitLab. It covers the fixed version for each PHP branch and distribution, how to use GitLab features to locate PHP projects across your groups, how to track remediation, and how to check for signs of compromise.

Upgrade PHP to a fixed version now

Upgrade the PHP runtime on every host and in every container image to a fixed version. Framework updates, Composer updates, input validation, and authentication don’t help, because PHP handles the request before application code runs.

BranchFixed in
PHP 8.5.x8.5.12
PHP 8.4.x8.4.27
PHP 8.3.x8.3.36
PHP 8.2.x8.2.35 (end of life December 31, 2026)
PHP 8.6 release candidates8.6.0RC4. The official php:8.6-rc image was still on RC3 on October 21, and RC3 does not have the fix.
PHP 8.1 and olderNo official release. PHP published minimal source backports for 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1, and some distributions ship patched packages.

If your PHP comes from a distribution package, upgrade that package. Fixed package versions as of October 22:

DistributionFixed package
Ubuntu 26.04php8.5 8.5.4-0ubuntu1.5
Ubuntu 24.04php8.3 8.3.6-0ubuntu0.24.04.13
Ubuntu 22.04php8.1 8.1.2-1ubuntu2.28
Debian 13php8.4 8.4.27-1~deb13u1
Debian 12php8.2 8.2.35-1~deb12u1
Alpine 3.24php83 8.3.36, php84 8.4.27, php85 8.5.12
RHEL 10php 8.3.36-1.el10_2 (RHSA-2026:87070), php8.4 8.4.27-1.el10_2 (RHSA-2026:87071)
RHEL 9php 8.0.30-8.el9_8.1 (RHSA-2026:87151), php:8.2 8.2.35-1 (RHSA-2026:87072), php:8.3 8.3.36-1 (RHSA-2026:87079); php:8.4 had no fix yet on October 22
RHEL 8php:7.4 7.4.33-8 (RHSA-2026:87080); check Red Hat’s CVE pages for php:8.2. Retired streams (7.2, 7.3, 8.0) get no fix

Sources: Ubuntu, Debian, Alpine, and Red Hat security trackers, as of October 22, 2026.

Ubuntu, and Red Hat for its 7.4 and 8.0 packages, keep the old upstream version number and backport the fix. Compare the package versions rather than php -v. Restart every process that runs PHP after upgrading.

Rebuild your container images. If your image uses a floating tag of the official php image, such as php:8, php:8.3, php:8.3-apache or php:latest, rebuild it with docker build --pull and redeploy it. Images that pin a patch version, such as php:8.3.35-apache, need the tag changed to the fixed version first. Images built on derivatives such as wordpress or drupal get the fix only after their maintainers publish an updated image, so check the upstream image before you rebuild.

Locate PHP projects across your GitLab groups

Any project that runs PHP to serve web requests needs a fixed version, including the ones that are easy to forget, such as an internal dashboard, a marketing site, or a CI job image. Finding them takes two views: a static search of what your repositories declare and your images contain, and a runtime inventory of what actually runs. GitLab covers the static view with two features. Use both, in this order.

1. Container scanning

Container scanning reports vulnerabilities in operating system packages, so it finds PHP installed with apt, apk, or dnf, and it reports the two CVEs once they reach the scanner’s vulnerability database. To turn it on for a project, add the template to .gitlab-ci.yml:

include:
  - template: Security/Container-Scanning.gitlab-ci.yml

You can also use a group-level scan execution policy to turn container scanning on for every project in a group at once. When a policy is enabled, the next time a pipeline is run, it will be run with container scanning. Container scanning results for the default branch can be reviewed in the Vulnerability Report after the scanner completes.

Additionally, you can set up Merge Request Approval policies with container scanning. With merge request approvals in play, if a code change contains PHP2Shell, the policy will block a merge without approval from the selected parties.

Container scanning detects only PHP installed as a package. PHP compiled from source, including the official php images, has no package record, so a project can pass container scanning and still run a vulnerable PHP. Code search covers that gap.

2. Code search

Exact code search can find the two types of files that indicate a PHP project. Run these at the top-level group with regular expression mode enabled (the .* toggle at the right of the search box):

  • Container base images: This query searches for every file GitLab detects as a Dockerfile. The pattern matches any image whose name or tag contains php, so it also finds derivatives such as wordpress, frankenphp, or bitnami/php-fpm. Expect a few false positives that you can rule out by reading the result: lang:Dockerfile ^FROM.*php
  • Composer projects: This query finds projects that use PHP even when they have no Dockerfile, or when the Dockerfile takes its image from a build argument such as FROM $BASE_IMAGE:
file:composer\.json$

Exact code search covers the default branch only. On GitLab.com it is on by default for paid plans. On GitLab Self-Managed instances an administrator must install Zoekt first. GitLab Dedicated doesn’t support exact code search.

For each result, confirm the version. You can check the FROM php: line, or run php -v in the running container, and compare it with the table above. The group dependency list shows Composer packages and framework versions but not the PHP runtime version.

3. Compare with your runtime inventory

Container scanning and code search show what your projects declare and build, not what runs. PHP can run outside your GitLab projects, for example on web servers with mod_php or PHP-FPM enabled only in their configuration, on hosts configured by hand, or in containers that still run in clusters without an active pipeline. Compare the static results with an inventory of your running workloads from your configuration management (Ansible, Puppet, Chef, etc.), cloud, or VM inventory tools. For Kubernetes, operational container scanning scans the images that run in your clusters, with the same package-only detection as container scanning. Treat every PHP runtime that appears in only one of the two views as a gap to investigate.

Remediate at scale with GitLab Duo Agent Platform

Start with asking GitLab Duo Agentic Chat to:

  • collect every container scanning finding for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 across the group from the vulnerability report (requires an Ultimate subscription)
  • run the code search queries above across the group, review each hit and read the PHP version from the Dockerfile or the Composer files
  • open a merge request per affected project that bumps the base image tag or the package to the fixed version, and assign it to the right maintainer
  • track the whole effort in an epic with one issue per project, and is closed when the fixed version is deployed and confirmed

From each issue, the Developer Flow can open a merge request that updates the base image tag or package to a fixed version. Turn on automatic reviews with the Code Review Flow to get a first review that follows your custom review instructions. Review and merge each merge request, then close the issue once the fixed version is deployed.

Searches find candidates, but a security or platform engineer still has to review each match, resolve CI includes, and tell what the code declares apart from what actually runs. An example agent skill from the GitLab Developer Advocacy team handles this work. It runs on GitLab Duo Agent Platform and with agents that use GitLab MCP server or the glab CLI, such as Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor.

The skill checks container images, CI jobs, OS packages, configuration management variables, Composer pins, and environments. It returns a cited findings table with deployment evidence, and open gaps. The skill is read-only: It makes no changes, and remediation merge requests remain a separate, reviewed step. It cannot confirm what is running on hosts it cannot access, so verify those directly. Adapt the skill to your own environment before you use it.

Check for compromise

Reports of exploitation differ. Security researchers reported an exploit attempt on October 17, 2026, before public disclosure, and further reports of exploitation followed the release. The PHP project identified no functional exploits at the time of release. If an internet-facing server ran a vulnerable PHP version, review its logs from October 17, 2026, onward for:

  • Multipart requests followed by memory-limit errors or repeated HTTP 500 responses
  • Unusually large or malformed PHPSESSID response cookies
  • Unexplained PHP worker restarts, or shell processes started by PHP workers
  • Unexpected files on the PHP web server, outbound connections from PHP workers, or unexpected cron entries

A successful exploit can return HTTP 200 and leave the worker running, so an absence of errors doesn’t rule out compromise. If you find signs of exploitation, isolate the server and start an incident investigation. Where possible, capture memory, disk, and logs before patching and restarting. Restarting PHP workers may erase evidence. CVE-2026-109619 can also expose process memory, even when an attacker doesn’t achieve code execution. Rotate any credentials, tokens, or keys the PHP process could read.

Note: Scanners may flag the Gemnasium dependency scanning image (gemnasium:6), deprecated since GitLab 17.9, for its bundled PHP. It is used only as a command-line tool and never handles HTTP requests, so it is not exploitable, and a fixed version has already shipped under the same tag.

DateWhat happened
August 1Calif discovers the first flaw during an AI-assisted PHP audit and reports it to PHP on August 11; Wiz Research independently finds and reports the flaws on August 24.
October 17Amazon’s honeypots record the first known exploit attempt, while the flaws are still under embargo.
October 20PHP announces that a security release fixing two critical vulnerabilities will ship on October 21.
October 20Vulnerability details leak before coordinated disclosure. (Huntress)
October 21, 14:00 UTCPHP releases 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35 and publishes the advisories.

title: Redesign how your team ships software with AI agents
summary:
AI agents are sending more and more code into review queues built for human-paced work. A coding assistant can speed up code writing, but it can’t show you whether review, security checks, and release approvals can keep pace with all that extra code. AI-native engineering — the practice of intentionally designing the engineering process so people and agents each do what they are best suited to — starts with identifying delivery bottlenecks, then deciding how much autonomy agents should have and how to maintain control as you scale.

The AI-Native Engineering Playbook, launching this week, helps teams turn faster coding into faster delivery by redesigning how they ship software with agents. Every practice in the playbook is grounded in insights from engineering leaders at GitLab, our customers, and members of our Software Engineering Leadership Forum (SELF) community. We also partnered with IT Revolution to incorporate findings from a diverse group of practitioners looking at AI-native software development from a number of different angles, from code review to agent autonomy.

Below are a few of the questions we sought to answer in the process of creating the playbook.

Where does the bottleneck go when coding gets faster?

Coding used to be the slowest, most expensive part of building software. Agents removed the bottleneck on coding, and the constraint moved to everything around the code: waiting for clarifications, environments, approvals, and other teams. GitLab’s AI Accountability Report, based on an April 2026 survey of 1,528 DevSecOps professionals, found that 79% of respondents agreed that individual developer productivity has improved with AI, but the overall software delivery process has not accelerated at the same pace.

Large enterprises typically have software delivery lead times of well over 200 days, with active development taking only 10% to 20% of that time. The numbers explain why a faster coding step is often disappointing in the long run. For example, imagine a 281-day delivery cycle that involves about 32 days spent on coding. Make coding 50% faster, and you save about 16 days, a 6% improvement. But if you take coding all the way to zero, around 88% of the lead time stays untouched. [1]

GitLab’s research similarly found that DevSecOps professionals reported spending only 16% of their time writing new code, and 85% agreed AI has shifted the bottleneck from writing code to reviewing and validating it.

That means your first job is diagnosis. Take one small, real change and trace it from request to production, marking every wait and every handoff. The longest waits show where your next improvement is, and it's rarely in the code. Watch where an agent stalls on a small task, too. The stall usually points to a standard nobody documented, an environment that’s hard to start, or context that lived in a single person’s head.

How much autonomy should agents have?

Agent autonomy should depend on how well you can verify the agent output. Imagine a ladder with four stages, ranging from semi-manual (a person approving every step) to fully autonomous (a zero-touch workflow). In this framework, there are clear rules for advancing up the ladder: no rungs can be skipped, and each step up needs to be backed with evidence from the rung below. [2]

  1. Stage 1: Humans are in the loop at every step
  2. Stage 2: Humans are still in the loop, but the agent executes within set bounds
  3. Stage 3: Humans are out of the loop for normal operation and handle only exceptions
  4. Stage 4: A zero-touch workflow, where the agent manages itself end to end, calling in a human only when predefined thresholds are met [2]

It’s also important for a named human to stay accountable for every AI-enabled workflow, and the line between a human reviewing and a human monitoring should be explicitly defined, since loose or arbitrary definitions tend to erode under time pressure. [3]

That erosion is the trap. A person who is nominally in the loop but approves everything gives the appearance of control without the benefits, and habit and volume can easily turn review into mindless rubber-stamping. A checkpoint nobody actually exercises is worse than none, because it creates confidence where the system needs scrutiny.

The way up is to earn each step on evidence. Set an explicit accuracy or success threshold before you widen a step, then move people from reviewing each step to monitoring the whole. An agent that stops more often to ask for help is a healthy sign, since the system is refusing to outrun its own evidence. [2]

How do you review code at agent volume?

Widening autonomy depends on catching mistakes, and that puts pressure on code review. Review at merge time was built for human-paced output. Agents raise the rate of change, and manual review of every change set has become unsustainable. GitLab’s research also highlighted this strain: 78% of respondents agreed existing code review processes were not designed for the scale of code AI tools enable, and 80% agreed their organization has adopted AI coding tools faster than it has developed policies to govern them.

The answer is a layered verification system in which each layer does the part it does best. Humans are only removed from the loop when the risk level and evidence justify that design choice — it’s never a default. [4]

  1. Move objective checks, such as formatting, types, and dependency policy, as close to authoring as possible.
  2. Keep changes small so every later layer works faster.
  3. Define the expected behavior up front so there is something concrete to check.
  4. Use an independent reviewer.
  5. Match review depth to the risk of the change.
  6. Record every agentic review decision in a form someone can inspect later.

The organizations that have been most successful here have already invested heavily in automated testing, static analysis, and small change sets, so the layers work best on a foundation you already have. [4]

Dive into the playbook, or contribute your own insights

Becoming AI-native is a practice that leaders will continue to refine with their teams as tools and understanding evolve. To get started, read the entire playbook, or begin with the part that matches where your team runs into the most friction:

  • Redesigning the work so agents fit the flow of delivery instead of attaching to steps built for people alone
  • Working with agents by deciding where human judgment and accountability stay and how engineers keep growing as the coding shifts
  • Governing and scaling from one workflow to many with the context, verification, and measurement that let you move faster without losing control of quality or risk

If you lead an engineering team and want to contribute your own insights to the playbook, join SELF, the community for engineering leaders navigating the AI era.

Enterprise Technology Leadership Journal 3, no. 2 (Fall 2026). https://itrevolution.com/product/when-coding-is-free/.
  2. Cockcroft, Adrian, and Jeremy Eder, Joseph Enochs, Jenn Spykerman, and Brian Wald. "When Agents Decide: Continuous Decision Intelligence and the Substrate Beneath It." Enterprise Technology Leadership Journal 3, no. 2 (Fall 2026). https://itrevolution.com/product/when-agents-decide/.
  3. Eslick, Ian, and Collin Fox, Amanda Graham, Suzette Johnson, Chuck Lafferty, Tom Kilcommons, Rosalind Radcliffe, Cat Swetel, Annie Vella, Sam Yeats, and Robin Yeman. "The Sociotechnical Architecture of AI-Enabled Enterprises: Principles, Patterns, and Practices for Human-Governed AI." Enterprise Technology Leadership Journal 3, no. 2 (Fall 2026). https://itrevolution.com/product/sociotechnical-architecture-of-ai-enabled-enterprises/.
  4. Davis, Zach, and Michelle Gill, Elisabeth Hendrickson, Angie Jones, Sha Ma, Randy Shoup, and James Wickett. "Agentic AI and Code Reviews: Toward a Pattern Language for Code Reviews in the Age of Agentic AI." GitLab’s AI Accountability Report, based on an April 2026 survey of 1,528 DevSecOps professionals, found that 79% of respondents agreed that individual developer productivity has improved with AI, but the overall software delivery process has not accelerated at the same pace.

Large enterprises typically have software delivery lead times of well over 200 days, with active development taking only 10% to 20% of that time. The numbers explain why a faster coding step is often disappointing in the long run. For example, imagine a 281-day delivery cycle that involves about 32 days spent on coding. Make coding 50% faster, and you save about 16 days, a 6% improvement. But if you take coding all the way to zero, around 88% of the lead time stays untouched. [1]

GitLab’s research similarly found that DevSecOps professionals reported spending only 16% of their time writing new code, and 85% agreed AI has shifted the bottleneck from writing code to reviewing and validating it.

That means your first job is diagnosis. Take one small, real change and trace it from request to production, marking every wait and every handoff. The longest waits show where your next improvement is, and it's rarely in the code. Watch where an agent stalls on a small task, too. The stall usually points to a standard nobody documented, an environment that’s hard to start, or context that lived in a single person’s head.

How much autonomy should agents have?

Agent autonomy should depend on how well you can verify the agent output. Imagine a ladder with four stages, ranging from semi-manual (a person approving every step) to fully autonomous (a zero-touch workflow). In this framework, there are clear rules for advancing up the ladder: no rungs can be skipped, and each step up needs to be backed with evidence from the rung below. [2]

  1. Stage 1: Humans are in the loop at every step
  2. Stage 2: Humans are still in the loop, but the agent executes within set bounds
  3. Stage 3: Humans are out of the loop for normal operation and handle only exceptions
  4. Stage 4: A zero-touch workflow, where the agent manages itself end to end, calling in a human only when predefined thresholds are met [2]

It’s also important for a named human to stay accountable for every AI-enabled workflow, and the line between a human reviewing and a human monitoring should be explicitly defined, since loose or arbitrary definitions tend to erode under time pressure. [3]

That erosion is the trap. A person who is nominally in the loop but approves everything gives the appearance of control without the benefits, and habit and volume can easily turn review into mindless rubber-stamping. A checkpoint nobody actually exercises is worse than none, because it creates confidence where the system needs scrutiny.

The way up is to earn each step on evidence. Set an explicit accuracy or success threshold before you widen a step, then move people from reviewing each step to monitoring the whole. An agent that stops more often to ask for help is a healthy sign, since the system is refusing to outrun its own evidence. [2]

How do you review code at agent volume?

Widening autonomy depends on catching mistakes, and that puts pressure on code review. Review at merge time was built for human-paced output. Agents raise the rate of change, and manual review of every change set has become unsustainable. GitLab’s research also highlighted this strain: 78% of respondents agreed existing code review processes were not designed for the scale of code AI tools enable, and 80% agreed their organization has adopted AI coding tools faster than it has developed policies to govern them.

The answer is a layered verification system in which each layer does the part it does best. Humans are only removed from the loop when the risk level and evidence justify that design choice — it’s never a default. [4]

  1. Move objective checks, such as formatting, types, and dependency policy, as close to authoring as possible.
  2. Keep changes small so every later layer works faster.
  3. Define the expected behavior up front so there is something concrete to check.
  4. Use an independent reviewer.
  5. Match review depth to the risk of the change.
  6. Record every agentic review decision in a form someone can inspect later.

The organizations that have been most successful here have already invested heavily in automated testing, static analysis, and small change sets, so the layers work best on a foundation you already have. [4]

Dive into the playbook, or contribute your own insights

Becoming AI-native is a practice that leaders will continue to refine with their teams as tools and understanding evolve. To get started, read the entire playbook, or begin with the part that matches where your team runs into the most friction:

  • Redesigning the work so agents fit the flow of delivery instead of attaching to steps built for people alone
  • Working with agents by deciding where human judgment and accountability stay and how engineers keep growing as the coding shifts
  • Governing and scaling from one workflow to many with the context, verification, and measurement that let you move faster without losing control of quality or risk

title: Uncover the business logic vulnerabilities SAST scanners miss
summary:
Broken object-level authorization ranks first on the OWASP API Security Top 10, and OWASP says that traditional static application security testing (SAST) tools struggle to find access control flaws. A missing authorization check is an absence of code, so a scanner that matches patterns has nothing to match. You can find the gap only if you already know what the endpoint is meant to enforce.

We're building Business Logic Security Analyzer in GitLab Duo Agent Platform to catch business logic vulnerabilities that pattern-based scanners miss. It is now in early access for GitLab Ultimate customers on GitLab.com.

Valid code, wrong intent

Any application security team will recognize these three findings:

  1. An endpoint takes an order ID from the request and returns the order without checking who owns it.
  2. A role field on a user profile accepts whatever JSON the client sends.
  3. A user ID is a sequential integer.

Each one is valid code that slips past most taint and pattern rules in a conventional SAST engine, because no untrusted data reaches a dangerous sink, and no known-bad signature appears. Chained together, they hand an attacker every customer's order and an administrator role.

Across GitLab's customer base, codebase size has grown as much as 500% as agents write code. CVE disclosures through April ran 46% above the February forecast from the Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams. The same AI models that generate code also make existing weaknesses less expensive to discover and chain. Authorization logic is where that pressure lands: Developers and agents write a check in a line or two, but when one is missing, the gap often goes unnoticed. As Omer Azaria, vice president of Product Management at GitLab, put it at GitLab Transcend, "We're caught in the middle: more code, faster attacks, same teams."

Why whole-repository scanning starts here

GitLab Duo Security Review looks for authorization flaws in merge requests, but many business logic flaws aren't visible in a diff. Whether an endpoint should check ownership depends on the data model, the roles the application defines, and how other endpoints treat the same records. Judging one handler means reading the application around it.

That is why Business Logic Security Analyzer scans the whole repository, and why GitLab is the platform to do it on. The source code, the pipelines that build it, the security findings attached to it, and the policies that gate it all live in one system. An agent that scans here sees the full application and writes its findings where the security team already works.

At Transcend, we introduced the GitLab Security Standard: five stages each agent must clear to earn more autonomy, built on the premise that code is now abundant and trust is scarce. Its Verify stage requires every change, whether written by a person or agent, to pass controls the author cannot touch. Business Logic Security Analyzer runs outside the author's hands, and its findings persist in the same report and dashboards that govern the rest of the codebase.

How the analyzer works

Business Logic Security Analyzer is a foundational flow on GitLab Duo Agent Platform that targets business logic flaws, starting with broken object-level authorization, missing or improper authorization, and mass assignment. A practitioner can run a whole-repository scan, and scan each merge request automatically after its pipeline passes.

Detecting any of these flaws requires a model of what the application is meant to do. Pattern scanners have none, but an agent that reads the repository can build one. The analyzer starts by enumerating the application’s entry points and mapping who should be allowed to do what: which records belong to which user, and which actions are administrative. It then reads each handler in scope and checks whether the handler enforces that rule before touching the record. Findings land in the Vulnerability Report and the merge request security widget as first-class SAST results, to support triage, remediation, and auditing.

In the demo application below, refund_order accepts an order_id from the request and sets refunded=1 without checking that the caller owns the order or is an administrator. Taint rules stay silent because the query is parameterized. The analyzer reports it as CWE-639, Critical, at app/orders.py:17, and its explanation names the missing ownership check.

The models behind the analyzer

Business Logic Security Analyzer is the first GitLab capability supporting Anthropic's Claude Mythos 5.1, and is available in early access to customers in approved environments. The model sees only GitLab's prompts and the customer's repository, which holds the context the analyzer needs: the data model, roles, and rules each endpoint enforces. As Rajat Pandit, Head of Applied AI, Anthropic India, said at Transcend, "When defenders have more context than attackers, advanced models change the math in their favor."

Alongside Mythos, the analyzer supports Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Sonnet 5, and Sonnet 4.6, with more models planned for future releases. All of them run as GitLab-managed models through GitLab’s AI gateway, under the same data handling terms as the rest of GitLab Duo Agent Platform.

Request early access

Business Logic Security Analyzer is in early access for a small group of GitLab Ultimate customers on GitLab.com. Participants run the analyzer on their codebases to find true positives their security teams didn’t already know about. We will work with each team to learn where the analyzer is correct, wrong, or silent. Each scan consumes GitLab Credits, and cost scales with the size of the application's attack surface.

To be considered, contact your account team, or, if you are not yet a GitLab customer, contact our sales team. Once your group is enabled, start a whole-repository scan from GitLab Duo Chat or through the API, and attach the Business Logic scan profile to a project to scan its merge requests. The Business Logic Security Analyzer documentation covers prerequisites and setup.

title: AI Governance: One view of agent activity
summary:
AI coding agents are writing and changing code, from GitLab Duo Agent Platform agents to externally connected agents like Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex. You are accountable for what those agents do, yet most of their activity stays invisible: which agents ran, who used them, and what they touched. Teams often struggle with understanding whether a developer used a tool or model that is approved or not.

The AI Governance Dashboard, now in beta, gives you one place to see agent activity across your top-level group. It brings GitLab Duo Agent Platform agents and the external agents your developers connect into one view, showing which agents ran, who used them, and which projects they touched. The dashboard also shows the tools and sessions associated with each agent.

With that audit trail in place, you can answer the questions auditors and risk owners ask: who ran this agent, what did it do, and who is accountable for it. Every agent action gets recorded in one audit trail, detailing the model it used, the tools it called, and the project it ran in. You can now investigate a session or hand an auditor evidence without stitching together multiple sources of data.

Watch a demo of the AI Governance Dashboard:

Gain visibility into AI agent activity

More AI agents are running across your organization than you can track by hand. GitLab Duo Agent Platform agents run inside GitLab, while externally connected agents like Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex run on developers' own machines.

The result is the shadow AI problem: real work happening in your projects, from many tools, that no one accountable can see in one place or tie to a team member.

The AI Governance Dashboard brings that activity into view and connects each agent to the developer behind it. To turn it on in your top-level group, go to AI > Governance. GitLab Duo Agent Platform agents and externally connected agents appear together, and you can toggle between the views to see all agents, just Duo Agent Platform Agents or just externally connected agents. Three tiles at the top give you a baseline: how many agents ran, how many sessions they started, and how many tool calls they made over the past seven or 30 days. Each tile shows the daily trend and the change from the previous period, so a spike, like a new tool your team started using last week, stands out. The cards below tell you where to act. You can check whether the agents your developers rely on match the ones you approved, see which projects carry the most agent activity and need closer review, and know who to talk to when usage shifts.

Prove what every agent did

Managing AI risk starts with knowing what every agent did and who prompted it. Traditional audit trails were built for human changes, so that record is often scattered across tools or missing. GitLab records every agent action as an audit event, so you can investigate an incident or answer an auditor from one place.

Open any GitLab Duo Agent Platform session to see the prompt the developer sent, the tools the agent called, the MCP servers it used, the model that ran, and the project it changed. From there, you can download an immutable copy of the session as evidence, or stream the events to your security information and event management (SIEM) system.

Set up your dashboard today

It only takes a few steps to set up the AI Governance Dashboard:

  1. Check access. The dashboard needs the Owner role on the top-level group, or a custom role with the read_agent_artifacts ability. If the people who should watch agent activity don’t have Owner access, create that custom role first.
  2. Turn on AI audit event storage. Storage is off by default, and events are only recorded after you turn it on. In your top-level group, go to Settings > GitLab Duo, select Change configuration, and then Store AI audit events in the Data and privacy section. You need to have an Owner or Security Manager role to have access.
  3. Open the dashboard. In your top-level group, go to AI > Governance, and select the Dashboard tab to see your GitLab Duo Agent Platform activity.
  4. Connect your externally connected agents. Sign in with GitLab CLI (glab) 1.122.0 or later on macOS or Linux. To capture Claude Code sessions, run glab govern setup, which installs the Claude Code hooks. To also capture Cursor and Codex sessions, run glab govern setup --agents codex,cursor, which adds a background job that sends those sessions every 30 minutes. Run glab govern doctor to confirm the setup works.

The AI Governance Dashboard is in beta for GitLab Premium and Ultimate customers. Turn it on for your top-level group to keep oversight of AI usage as fast as your teams adopt it.

Not on GitLab yet? Try GitLab Ultimate for free and use the AI Governance Dashboard to get started.

title: Three developer tasks worth handing to an agent
summary:
You already have an AI assistant. It completes your code, explains code you didn’t write, and maybe even drafts a whole feature while you sip your coffee. An agent on GitLab picks up where your editor stops.

The AI in your editor only knows what's open in your editor. It doesn't know that your merge request has been sitting in the queue for two days, or that your pipeline failed for the third time this week. Without your pipeline logs, it can’t offer a fix.

GitLab Duo Agent Platform works within the project and across your software delivery workflow, taking into account merge requests, issues, pipelines, and repositories your whole team shares. This context makes all the difference.

Here are three ways to try out GitLab’s agentic features today, and you don't need a paid GitLab plan to do it.

Set up your group

On GitLab.com, a group Owner sets up your top-level group:

  • Purchase GitLab Credits.
    • Go to Settings > Billing and select Purchase credits.
  • Turn on GitLab Duo Agent Platform.
  • Turn on foundational flows.
    • Go to Settings > GitLab Duo.
      • Select Change configuration.
      • Under Flow execution, select Allow flow execution and Allow foundational flows.
      • Select Code Review and Fix CI/CD Pipeline.
      • Select Save changes.

1. Hand off the first pass on reviews

Code Review Flow reads a merge request's diff, description, and related files (like tests and dependencies), then posts detailed review comments directly on the merge request. The flow catches small issues, missed edge cases, and inconsistent patterns on your merge requests, so you can save your judgment for the critical details.

Try it on your project:

  1. On a merge request, assign @GitLabDuo as a reviewer, or comment /assign_reviewer @GitLabDuo.
  2. Watch the review comments appear on the merge request itself, the same place your teammates will see them. Code Review Flow checks the diff, the description, and related files like tests and dependencies before it comments.

To hand off the first pass on every new merge request, turn on automatic reviews.

Watch how merge requests can speed up with Code Review Flow:

2. Send a failed pipeline to an agent to investigate

Have Fix CI/CD Pipeline Flow diagnose your failed pipeline and propose a fix, so you spend your time applying it instead of hunting for the cause.

This flow investigates logs, error messages, the merge request changes that likely caused it, and the repository contents. Depending on the failure, it either proposes an inline code suggestion on your merge request or opens a new merge request with a fix.

Try it on your project:

  1. On a merge request with a failing pipeline, select Fix pipeline with Duo from the Overview or Pipelines tab. The flow reads the pipeline logs and your merge request changes to find the cause.
  2. Select AI > Sessions to follow along, then review the result on your merge request. Depending on the failure, you get inline code suggestions you can apply, a new merge request if the fix touches files outside your diff, or a comment with next steps when a failure needs a person.

For pipelines that aren't tied to a merge request, you can trigger the same flow: go to Build > Pipelines, select the failing pipeline, and select Fix pipeline with Duo. You get a new merge request with the fix.

Follow along with this demo:

3. Get answers from across your project

Ask Agentic Chat what changed in a merge request or why last night's pipeline failed, and get one answer that pulls from your project's merge requests, issues, and pipelines. This is where most editor-based AI assistants fall short. Your IDE's assistant can tell you what a function does, but it can't tell you which issue introduced it or why last night's pipeline failed.

Try it on your project:

  1. In the GitLab UI, open your project. In the GitLab Duo sidebar, select Add new chat, then select an agent. You can also use Agentic Chat in VS Code, JetBrains IDEs, and Visual Studio.
  2. Make sure the Agentic toggle is turned on.
  3. Ask what you'd normally dig for by hand. Agentic Chat searches your project's issues and merge requests by keyword and retrieves pipelines to build its answer. For ready-made prompts, browse the AI Resource Library, for example Summarize Recent Changes to MR/Issue or Debug Failing Pipeline.

You can also ask Agentic Chat to run either flow above on a merge request. Each chat message you send uses GitLab Credits.

Watch the demo:

What these agentic features cost

On GitLab Free, you can use a set of GitLab Duo Agent Platform agents and flows, including all three above, without upgrading to Premium or Ultimate. Your group buys a monthly commitment pool of GitLab Credits that every group member draws from, so you pay for the work agents and flows do instead of paying per seat. The pool refreshes each month on an annual term. You can increase it at any time and decrease it at renewal.

Each feature uses credits at its own rate. For Agentic Chat and Fix CI/CD Pipeline Flow, usage depends on the model and on how much back-and-forth a request needs. The credit multiplier tables list current rates. Buying the pool also turns on on-demand billing for usage beyond it, so set usage caps to control spend.

Where to start

If you only try one this week, make it the Code Review Flow. Assign @GitLabDuo as a reviewer on your next merge request and see what it comes up with. From there, Agentic Chat and Fix CI/CD Pipeline Flow are ready to be deployed when you are.

Ready to get started? You can purchase GitLab Credits for your monthly commitment pool in your Customer Portal.

title: Building AI security in the open
summary:
When code becomes abundant trust becomes scarce.

That is the argument GitLab CEO Bill Staples made in his recent essay: AI is collapsing the cost of producing software, and everything around production, including context, verification, governance, and evidence, becomes proportionally more important. Both security and collaboration are key elements to producing trust. AI widens what has to be trusted to include the agents that now write software along with the software that gets written.

That is why GitLab is joining the Open Secure AI Alliance, which brings together organizations to develop and share open technologies, techniques, and tools that help safeguard software and agents in the age of AI. We joined because we believe AI security is strongest when it can be inspected, tested, adapted, and improved by a broad community of defenders.

This is an extension of work GitLab is already doing in the open.

GitLab’s AI Gateway is a standalone service that provides access to AI features across GitLab.com, GitLab Dedicated, and self-managed instances. Its source code is public, and so are the agent workflow configurations running on AI Gateway, including configurations for code creation, code review, secrets false-positive detection, and security review.

  • Developer Flow configuration
  • Code Review Flow configuration
  • Security Review Flow

These examples reflect an important principle: An AI system is more than the model behind it. Trust depends on the surrounding harness, workflows, controls, context, and evaluation. Open tooling makes it easier for defenders to understand how those pieces work, test them against real risks, and improve them over time.

We also believe enterprises need choice. Organizations should be able to use proprietary and secure open weight models, select the right model for the job, and make decisions about where and how AI systems operate. Model and cloud agnosticism helps preserve that flexibility, while an open ecosystem gives customers more options for building, governing, and securing AI.

Transparency also has to cover the risks. Our documentation on security threats in agentic systems sets out the attack paths that apply to our own agents and the controls that apply in each environment. We treat our agents as privileged actors: Each one runs with an explicit identity, constrained tools and permissions, and actions that can be audited. We share how this works through our documentation for composite identity, sandboxed execution, per-flow tool restrictions, and agent tool governance.

Through our participation in the Open Secure AI Alliance, GitLab has an opportunity to share practical work already underway across our AI and security teams and learn from the broader community. Our goal is not to position open weight and closed models as opposites. It is to help ensure that defenders have the transparency, control, and flexibility they need to build trustworthy AI systems.

AI security should be built in the open. Learn more about the Open Secure AI Alliance.

title: GitLab Secrets Manager: Govern secrets like your code
summary:
Credentials often start in an engineer's local dev environments, then get copied into unscoped CI/CD variables to keep pipelines running. Stored there as a raw value rather than a reference to a scoped secret, a signing key reaches every job in the pipeline — compromised or not.

Standing up a standalone vault narrows that exposure but requires mirroring every change to project membership, protected branches, and production environments. When the vault falls out of sync, a pipeline breaks or an agent’s service account keeps access it no longer needs.

GitLab Secrets Manager tightens credential security without a second permission model. It is now generally available in GitLab 19.5 for Premium and Ultimate on GitLab.com and GitLab Self-Managed, with GitLab Dedicated coming soon. Built on OpenBao, it stores build-time and runtime credentials under the same permissions and audit trail as your code. Platform teams can offer developers self-service secrets, and security teams get credentials scoped to the jobs that use them, plus the pipeline and job ID on every CI/CD read.

"GitLab Secrets Manager lets us centralize secrets across CI/CD, Kubernetes, and infrastructure as code without standing up multiple vaults or maintaining separate integration points. It also strengthens our supply chain security by tightening which users and pipelines can access a given credential." - Jeremy Nauta, Software Architect, OneTrust

How Secrets Manager scopes build-time secrets to each job

Agents can take actions no one anticipated, so security teams need to regard every job as if its agents will use any credential it can reach. Secrets Manager narrows what agents can reach with the context GitLab already holds about each job: its project, the branch it runs on, whether that branch is protected, and the environment it targets.

A developer declares the secret a job needs with the secrets: keyword in .gitlab-ci.yml, and GitLab injects the value only into jobs that declare it and fall within its scope. Scope conditions accept wildcards on branch and environment, and they combine, so one rule can require a protected branch and a production/* environment before a job receives the credential.

Inside the job, GitLab writes the value to a temporary file and exposes only its path, which limits exposure in subprocesses, crash dumps, and telemetry. GitLab masks the value in job logs and discards it when the job ends. Unlike a CI/CD variable, a secret is never readable in your project configuration. OpenBao encrypts secrets at rest with AES-256-GCM, so a copy of the secrets database holds only ciphertext. Jobs fetch values straight from OpenBao with short-lived tokens bound to each job’s identity, which keeps plaintext secrets out of the GitLab application.

See how to get started with Secrets Manager:

Revoke and trace an exposed credential

When the axios npm package was compromised, a SANS advisory warned teams to "assume all environment variables on affected systems were exfiltrated" and extend investigations to CI/CD runners and build infrastructure. Responders had to work out which credentials each affected job could read, how to cut off access, and which runs read them.

With Secrets Manager, when a job runs a poisoned dependency, the exposure stops at the secrets that job declared and was authorized to read. To clean up, revoke and replace the leaked credential, update the value in Secrets Manager, and audit that one job while other pipelines keep running. Secrets Manager prompts you to set a rotation reminder when you create a secret. Dynamic credentials are coming soon and will provide ephemeral access without manual rotation.

GitLab streams every secret create, read, update, and delete event to your audit event destinations and records changes in the audit trail. Each pipeline read carries the pipeline and job IDs, which tie to the commit, the triggering user, and the merge request, when there is one. Incident responders and auditors can trace a read to the change behind it without correlating logs from a CI system, a vault, and an identity provider. Audit events never contain secret values.

Govern secrets with the permissions that govern your code

As agents take on more work, platform teams field more requests for pipelines and service accounts that need credentials. When those requests queue, teams fall back on broad grants and shared secrets.

Secrets Manager uses the GitLab namespace as its isolation boundary. Projects inherit secrets defined in the groups above them, so you define a shared credential once. Owners grant read, write, and delete permissions to specific users or default roles, using the same membership model that governs the code. Remove a person or an agent's service account from a project, and that identity's access to the project's secrets ends.

Developers reference secrets through the project access they already hold. When a secret reference breaks, they fix it in the same merge request as the code, with no second repository, approver, or access ticket. With a governed credential one line away, fewer secrets end up in over-scoped CI/CD variables, local files, or the repository.

One store for pipelines and runtime workloads

Kubernetes, Terraform, and scripts often get separate secret stores, each with its own access model and logs. Secrets Manager serves runtime tools from the same store as pipelines, under the same permissions and audit trail:

  • Kubernetes, through External Secrets Operator. ESO re-fetches the secret on a set interval and updates the Kubernetes Secret in place, so a rotated value reaches the cluster without a pipeline run.
  • Terraform and OpenTofu. They read a secret as a data source at plan or apply time and keep credentials out of .tfvars files and CI/CD variables.
  • OpenBao and Vault CLIs, through the Vault-compatible API. Teams keep their existing scripts and point them at Secrets Manager.
  • Other runtime tools, through the Secrets Manager API.

Each runtime tool authenticates with a service account or an access token, and that identity needs project membership and explicit read permission for the secret. GitLab then issues a separate token, valid for five minutes, that the tool uses to fetch it.

How Secrets Manager fits with GitLab's supply chain controls

GitLab’s governed software factory connects code, pipelines, packages, and secrets on one platform, with one identity model and one record of how a change reached production. Dependency Firewall decides which packages enter a pipeline, Secrets Manager limits which credentials the pipeline can reach, and Artifact Central governs what you ship.

Secrets Manager supports two of the five stages in the GitLab Security Standard, GitLab's framework for letting agents earn autonomy: For Authorize, it binds each job to the secrets its identity and scope allow, and for Respond, it streams every CRUD event.

Secret push protection blocks commits containing credentials before they reach the repository, and Secret detection finds the ones already in your code and history. GitLab Duo Agent Platform triages what those scans find and flags likely false positives, so your team revokes, rotates, and audits only real leaks.

GitLab's existing integrations for HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, and Google Cloud Secret Manager keep working alongside Secrets Manager, so you can migrate at your own pace.

Get started

GitLab Secrets Manager is a paid add-on for Premium and Ultimate, billed through GitLab Credits: 1 credit per secret stored per month, and 1 credit per 2,500 read operations. An enterprise license agreement is available for air-gapped environments.

  • On GitLab.com, top-level group Owners can try GitLab Secrets Manager free for 30 days or 500 evaluation credits, whichever ends first. Go to your top-level group, select Secure > Secrets Manager, then Start 30-day trial.
  • On GitLab Self-Managed, your administrator must install and enable Secrets Manager, following the documented sizing and high-availability guidance.
  • GitLab Dedicated support is coming soon.

To find the first credentials to move, run the secret audit tool for CI/CD variables, which flags variables likely to hold credentials. A migration workflow for CI/CD variables is in development.

Have suggestions or feedback? Share them in the Secrets Manager feedback issue.

title: Get every merge request in front of the right reviewer, faster
summary:
The code is written. Now who reviews it?

The volume of code has never been greater, but delivery hasn’t kept pace. At Meta, code changes on internal platforms grew 220% year over year, while changes that reached users as new features grew only 36% (Reuters, August 2026). Every one of those changes has to clear review before it reaches users.

Automated review absorbs much of that load. Code Review Flow in GitLab Duo Agent Platform reviews merge requests as they arrive, follows custom review instructions you define per project, and costs a flat 0.25 GitLab Credits per review ($0.25 at list price). If a manual review takes about 15 minutes of a senior engineer’s time, that’s roughly $25 per review, so automated review cuts per-review cost by 99% (GitLab).

Automated review doesn’t take people out of the loop. Approval rules, CODEOWNERS, and compliance policies still require a person to sign off on many changes. For those merge requests, the first slowdown is often finding the right reviewer, and it happens before anyone reads a line. The right reviewer needs expertise in the code being changed, room in their queue, and availability in a time zone where they can respond quickly. When authors can’t see those factors, a few senior engineers carry most of the reviews while other qualified reviewers sit idle.

GitLab 19.5 removes that step with Recommend Reviewers Flow. When you create a merge request, GitLab recommends the best individual reviewer based on workload, time zone, availability, and expertise defined by approval rules and CODEOWNERS. The flow explains why it chose that reviewer and lets you assign them in one click. Across your engineering organization, reviews start sooner, review load spreads across every qualified engineer, and more of the code your team writes reaches users.

Watch Recommend Reviewers Flow in action:

Review is a routing problem, not a headcount problem

Teams often treat slow reviews as a people problem. They add reminders, review rotations, extended time zone coverage, and escalations. Those workarounds cost people time and can lead to burnout, and they leave the real cause untouched: routing. The expertise and capacity already exist; there’s just nothing to match them to each merge request as it arrives.

Without that match, the author has to answer questions GitLab already can. Who knows this part of the codebase? Who has room in their queue? Who is online right now? Authors fall back on habits that slow everyone down:

  • Assigning a whole group. Everyone gets notified, nobody feels responsible, and the merge request waits for a volunteer.
  • Defaulting to the same trusted reviewer. That person becomes a bottleneck, and their own work stalls.
  • Guessing across time zones. The reviewer you picked just signed off for the day, so your feedback arrives tomorrow.

Reviewers pay a price, too. Group assignments flood their notifications with merge requests they will never review, which makes the ones that need them easier to miss. And the reviewers everyone defaults to absorb a growing share of the queue on top of their own work, which wears them down faster.

How intelligent reviewer suggestions work

GitLab Duo Agent Platform runs Recommend Reviewers Flow on your merge request and does the research for you:

  1. You create your merge request. A trigger starts the flow automatically when a merge request is created, whether in draft or ready state, so suggestions arrive from the start.
  2. The flow evaluates eligible reviewers. It weighs each candidate’s workload, time zone, availability, and expertise as defined by approval rules and CODEOWNERS, to find the person best suited and positioned to respond.
  3. You see the recommendation and the reasoning. The flow explains why it chose each reviewer, so you can approve the suggestion based on that context.
  4. You assign with one click. Suggestions appear in a dedicated panel on the merge request. You decide who reviews and when.

This design keeps you in control of timing. You can finish iterating or address automated code review feedback first, then bring in a human reviewer when the change is truly ready. You set it up as a flow trigger in your project rather than a project setting, so it fits alongside the other agentic workflows your team already runs.

What your team gains

The right reviewer match means faster feedback, clearer accountability, and a more balanced workload. Recommend Reviewers Flow makes that call consistently, at scale, and with reasoning you can see and override.

Recommend Reviewers Flow also works alongside the other foundational flows in GitLab Duo Agent Platform that handle the work around a merge request:

  • Run Code Review Flow first, so automated feedback lands before a person is brought in.
  • Add Security Review Flow to check merge request changes for business logic vulnerabilities before they merge.
  • Use Fix CI/CD Pipeline Flow to diagnose and repair failed jobs, so a broken pipeline doesn’t hold up an approved change.
  • Use Custom Flows to build Recommend Reviewers Flow into the process your team already follows.

Each step from merge request to merge runs on the same platform, under the same policies, so more of the code your team writes actually reaches users.

Get started

Intelligent reviewer suggestions are generally available in GitLab 19.5 for GitLab.com, GitLab Self-Managed, and GitLab Dedicated. To try them, add the Recommend Reviewers Flow trigger to your project, then create your next merge request. Learn more in our documentation.

New to GitLab Duo Agent Platform? Start a free trial today. Already a GitLab Premium or Ultimate subscriber? Turn on Duo Agent Platform and use the GitLab Credits included with your subscription.

title: Connect your agents to your software lifecycle with the GitLab MCP server
summary:
Agents are working across your team's software development lifecycle, but most still operate as separate tools, leaving the context, handoffs, and permissions for your team to stitch together. When your agents use APIs for these disparate tools, they often guess at endpoints and use up their context window on extra calls. The GitLab MCP server, now generally available with GitLab 19.5, connects your team’s external agents to your entire software lifecycle — from planning through production.

The GitLab MCP server enables any MCP-compatible agent to run GitLab workflows from the client your team already works in, getting what it needs in fewer calls and with less context bloat. Agents can work across code, merge requests, work items, and pipelines, and hand work to agentic flows within GitLab Duo Agent Platform. Each action runs under your existing GitLab permissions.

Built for how agents work

APIs are built for developers writing code. An agent that uses one has to work out which endpoints to call and make several calls to assemble one answer. Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard built for agents. An MCP server tells an agent what it can do and offers a curated set of tools designed around real workflows. Agents get the tools they need with more focused context, in fewer calls, and needing less data to carry through each task.

The GitLab MCP server applies that approach to your workflows across your projects, supporting all your team members within the GitLab permissions you already set.

Whether you're a developer handing a task to an agent or a team deciding how agents should work across your organization, your agents get tool coverage broad enough to complete the work, with access that follows each user’s GitLab permissions. Developers can even start GitLab Duo Agent Platform flows from the MCP-compatible coding agent they already use.

Here is Claude Code using the GitLab MCP server to start the Fix Pipeline flow in Duo Agent Platform:

More of your workflow, within reach of an agent

In addition to the tools announced in 19.4, the GitLab MCP server now includes more tools for working with code and pipelines, and for finding the right group or doc.

  • Code: add_branch starts a feature branch, get_repository_file reads a file at any ref, and semantic_search finds code by meaning, answering "where is this implemented?" without knowing the file or symbol name.
  • Pipelines: get_pipeline shows why a pipeline is red, with its jobs, downstream pipelines, and artifacts on request. list_pipelines surfaces patterns across recent runs, and get_artifact_file reads a single file from a job's artifacts, such as a log, report, or test fixture, without downloading the whole archive.
  • Orientation: list_groups lets an agent browse your group hierarchy to find the right group instead of guessing at identifiers, and list_wiki_pages, an opt-in tool, surfaces runbooks and docs before it answers a how-to question.

In 19.5, the MCP server tool catalog is also simpler to work with. Related tools are now consolidated, with fewer tools doing more. get_merge_request lets you ask your agent for a merge request’s commits, diffs, pipelines, conflicts, or notes. get_pipeline now includes get_pipeline_jobs, so you can ask for a pipeline’s jobs along with the pipeline itself. Your agents spend less time choosing the right tool and pull in only the details a task needs.

Toolsets let you choose which groups of tools the server returns. Each agent works from a focused set of tools that fits your team’s workflow instead of everything the server offers. A smaller set makes it less likely that an agent picks the wrong tool and has to retry. Most groups are on by default, and code security and wikis are available as opt-in groups. Browse the full catalog in the tools reference.

Start GitLab flows without leaving your client

Calling tools is one way an agent works with GitLab. Now, an agent can also hand a job to GitLab Duo Agent Platform and follow that job to the result without leaving your client. It can find the flows a project offers with list_duo_agents_and_flows, start a new flow from a goal in plain language with start_duo_session, and check progress with get_duo_session and list_duo_sessions. The work runs in a CI job inside GitLab, under the same context layer, policy checks, and audit trail as any other Duo Agent Platform session.

When a session needs a decision, it pauses for your input. With send_duo_session_input, you approve or reject the agent’s proposed action, or answer its question, and the session picks back up, keeping you in the loop. The duo_agent_platform toolset is included by default alongside the rest of the GitLab MCP server's tools.

Connect your agents to GitLab today

The agents supporting your software lifecycle will continue evolving. As your team adopts new agents, the GitLab MCP server connects each one to GitLab’s tools and flows, so they’re productive from day one.

You can connect the agents your team already uses by following the MCP server documentation, which includes setup instructions for Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, OpenAI Codex, Gemini, Kiro, Zed, and other MCP-compatible clients. The GitLab MCP server is available on the Free, Premium, and Ultimate tiers, on GitLab.com, GitLab Self-Managed, and GitLab Dedicated. On GitLab.com, per-user rate limits are set at 60 calls per minute on Free and 600 on Premium and Ultimate.

title: Unblock agentic software delivery with governed code review
summary:
AI agents have changed how much code a team can produce in a day. Review queues haven’t kept up, and delivery stalls while changes wait for a closer look. The usual workarounds (reminders, reviewer rotations, assigning a team) buy a little time and then burn people out.

Client-side review with AI helps the author by catching issues as the code is being written, before a merge request even opens. But it only goes so far. A review that only checks quality still leaves the organization without enforceable policy on the way to production, since comments on a diff do not decide whether a change can merge or reach production.

Every merge request still needs a consistent certification step tied to pipelines, security findings, code owners, approval rules, and audits. Review in the author’s environment cannot standardize that work across all your projects, route policy-bound changes to the right person, or show leaders what the agent did before the change merges. As agents write more of the code, automated reviews need to happen in the platform that already tracks each change from plan to production, and where identity, policy, and oversight controls are already in place.

Earlier this year, we made Code Review Flow generally available on GitLab Duo Agent Platform, bringing that sign-off to the merge request and making agentic review part of the same platform where code ships. Teams can turn it on so every change is automatically addressed under rules you set once, at $0.25 per review, delivering an estimated 100x ROI. That predictable unit cost is low enough to leave automatic review on for every merge request, which is how reviews move at machine speed while staying cost-efficient at organizational scale.

Agentic reviews, built for how you ship

Code Review Flow is native to GitLab merge requests, so it covers your whole environment. It runs as a CI/CD job on your runners, whether GitLab-hosted or your own, so review executes in the same environment as the rest of delivery. It works the same way on GitLab.com, GitLab Dedicated, and GitLab Self-Managed, keeping inference under your control with self-hosted models when air-gapped or regulated environments require it. You also have the flexibility to choose which model acts as the foundation for agentic code review: GitLab-managed or your own self-hosted models.

When certification is the default on the merge request, teams get coverage, control, and follow-through in one place. Here are the key highlights for agentic code review with GitLab Duo Agent Platform:

Every merge request is reviewed, without anyone having to ask. Turn on automatic reviews at the project, group, or instance level and settings cascade. Authors don’t have to remember to request a first pass.

Standards you set once for how the group ships. Custom review instructions capture language conventions, security practices, and path-specific rules. A group can point the Code Review Flow at a template project so those standards travel with the work. Pair guidance with GitLab’s enforced security and compliance controls when a requirement must always hold.

Follow-through on every finding. Follow-up review rechecks what GitLab Duo Agent Platform already flagged, verifies fixes, and avoids repeating the same points. At that price, you can leave automatic reviews everywhere.

The right human, when policy requires one. Code owners and relevant approval rules still apply. Recommend Reviewers Flow suggests the smallest group that can satisfy those rules based on their level of expertise, workload, availability, and timezone.

How agentic code review works in GitLab

Within GitLab, code review happens on the merge request, next to your pipelines, security findings, and approvals.

  1. A merge request opens (or becomes ready). Automatic review can start the Code Review Flow, or an author assigns GitLab Duo.
  2. The flow runs as a CI/CD job on your runners, analyzes the change with repository and merge request context, guided by your custom review instructions and the models your group selected, and comments on the diff.
  3. Authors and their coding agents push fixes. Follow-up review verifies Duo’s prior findings and carries context forward from the earlier pass.
  4. When a human must approve, Recommend Reviewers Flow proposes who should take the request; you assign from the merge request.
  5. Pipelines, security findings, approval rules, and the session record stay in the same place, so “reviewed” means certified on the path to production.

Watch agentic code review in GitLab in action:

What’s ahead

Our platform roadmap for agentic code review includes:

Deeper review when the change warrants it. An extended analysis pass will pull in calling code and tests for high-complexity merge requests, under your model-selection controls.

Clearer decisions on the merge request. GitLab Duo will be able to approve or request changes under settings you control.

Focus on risk. Risk assessment on the merge request will help teams see which changes deserve more attention.

Review before the merge request opens. Local review in Duo CLI will let developers run project review guidance against working-tree changes before the merge request runs the organization’s official check.

As agents write more of your code, you need reviewed code reaching production, with every change held to your standards and your reviewers focused on the changes that need a person. Every improvement on this roadmap is built to help you get there.

Getting started

title: Gemini 4 Argon on GitLab: Built for long-running agentic work
summary:
As AI models take on longer, multi-step work, the challenge is putting that power to use across the software lifecycle without adding risk or cost. Teams need to be able to move faster, within enterprise controls and guardrails.

Google's Gemini 4 Argon, now available on GitLab Duo Agent Platform, was built for that kind of work. With Argon, your team can delegate long, multi-step actions and receive outputs for review. In GitLab's internal evaluation, Gemini 4 Argon completed 93.3% of GitLab’s software engineering benchmark tasks.

Reliable execution for long-horizon tasks

Work across the software lifecycle demands persistence and steady attention. Argon sustains its reasoning across the many steps of a task, reading files, running commands, and editing code through to completion. Your engineers can delegate to GitLab Duo agents powered by Argon with confidence and spend their time reviewing results instead of monitoring runs.

Google trained Argon to respect system boundaries, tell you when it couldn't find something or finish a task, and pause for confirmation before an irreversible step. Teams can hand off complex tasks and stay in control of the important decisions.

In internal evaluations, Argon resolved 73.3% of GitLab’s benchmark tasks, with each change passing the benchmark’s tests across multiple programming languages. Of the runs that hit a tool error or timeout, Argon still completed 93.8% of them, so a single failure mid-run won’t force your team to start over. Agent output lands in a merge request, where your team reviews the result with the full context of the change.

Argon works through problems thoroughly, making it a strong model choice when finishing correctly matters more than finishing fast.

Choose the Gemini model that fits your workload

Gemini 4 Argon is Google's newest frontier model and the most performant Gemini model on GitLab Duo Agent Platform. It handles long-horizon agentic actions especially well, including tasks that begin loosely defined. It pairs with the Flash models, which offer a lower-cost option for high-volume work, so you can match each workload to the best Gemini model. Whichever Gemini model you choose, it runs inside the same context layer, policy checks, and audit trail that cover every agentic action across your software lifecycle.

title: Scaling Git for the agentic software factory
summary:
AI agents are fundamentally changing the economics of software development. As the cost of producing code falls, the volume of changes moving through the software factory is accelerating beyond what infrastructure designed for human developers was built to handle.

GitLab anticipated this shift and began developing next-generation source code management (SCM) to support thousands of concurrent agents working against large repositories. In June, we announced next-gen SCM at GitLab Transcend, joined on stage by Nick G. from Anthropic's source control team. We've continued collaborating on the technical challenges of agent-scale development, and in August we shared more of our architecture and early performance results.

This week, Anthropic provided a compelling demonstration of why this work is so important. As daily merges to its monorepo grew from approximately 2,500 in May to more than 30,000 in September, its engineers built Scion, a specialized source control system designed for their environment.

Anthropic's experience reinforces the architectural direction we've been pursuing. Scion is purpose-built for enormous monorepos where nearly all clients are agents that are always online. Anthropic acknowledges that its approach isn't a general-purpose replacement for Git and requires its own code review, search, and CI infrastructure.

GitLab is building for the broader enterprise market: delivering agent-scale performance while preserving Git compatibility, infrastructure choice, and integration with the software development lifecycle.

"Scaling our monorepo for agentic development has changed how we think about Git server architecture. We see room to expand what Git servers can do for these workloads without departing from the overall Git model."

— Nick G., Source Control, Anthropic

Built on Git. Designed for agents.

Traditional Git workflows require clients to download substantial repository data, even when an agent needs only a small portion. A single agent invocation can involve 5–10 GB of data transfer and more than 30 seconds of setup, just to answer one question. Multiply that overhead across thousands of agents and source control becomes a bottleneck.

Most enterprises can't move source control onto new infrastructure just to scale it. Next-gen SCM preserves the Git protocol while modernizing the architecture underneath. Stateless compute scales horizontally against shared object storage, while agent-native interfaces let agents request the files and history they need without repeatedly cloning entire repositories.

In early internal tests, workloads completed up to 50x faster, used up to 2x fewer tokens, and generated up to 1,000x less network traffic compared with conventional workflows.
